content.title: About
content.content: Beef, pot roast is a cut of beef—usually chuck or shoulder—slow‑cooked in a covered pot with a small amount of liquid, resulting in tender, flavorful, and juicy meat. It is commonly served with vegetables and a rich gravy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pot roast is a classic dish in American home cooking and is often associated with comfort food.
Low‑and‑slow cooking breaks down connective tissue, making the meat melt‑in‑your‑mouth tender.
Herbs such as rosemary, thyme, and bay leaf are frequently added for extra aroma.
Traditional pot roasts are made in heavy‑bottomed Dutch ovens, cast‑iron pots, or slow cookers.
Leftover pot roast works great in soups, stews, and sandwiches.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed and supports healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc in beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pot roast supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Beef fits well into low‑carb and ketogenic eating patterns.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Some cuts can be high in saturated fat, so choosing leaner portions is advisable.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may contain harmful bacteria such as E. coli or salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A small number of people may have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Beef contains purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pot roast as a main course with mashed potatoes, carrots, and onions, slice it for sandwiches, add it to salads, or shred it into tacos. Leftovers keep well in the fridge and can be incorporated into soups and stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pot roast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before serving.
